create-deleted-data

create-deleted-data.Rmd

Motivation

When we receive an updated version of a dataset, dfdiffs helps us answer three questions:

  1. What rows are here now that weren’t here before?
  2. What rows were here before that aren’t here now?
  3. What values have been changed?

This vignette covers create_deleted_data(), which answers the second question: “What rows were here before that aren’t here now?”

Packages 

library(dfdiffs)
library(flextable)

What rows were here before that aren’t here now?

We’ll use three datasets from the package to test for deleted data: CompleteData, IncompleteData, and DeletedData.

DeletedData

DeletedData contains the 4 rows removed from CompleteData to create IncompleteData, so it’s the result we expect create_deleted_data() to return:

We can confirm that combining IncompleteData and DeletedData recreates CompleteData:

combined <- rbind(IncompleteData, DeletedData)
combined <- combined[do.call(order, combined), ]
complete <- CompleteData[do.call(order, CompleteData), ]
all.equal(combined, complete, check.attributes = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

Arguments

create_deleted_data() takes the same compare, base, by, by_col, and cols arguments as create_new_data(). The reference table in that vignette lists every combination.

The only difference between the two functions is the direction of the anti join. create_new_data() looks for compare rows missing from base, and create_deleted_data() does the mirror image: it looks for base rows missing from compare.

create_deleted_data()

The signature for create_deleted_data() is below. It returns a data frame of the deleted rows.

create_deleted_data <- function(compare, base, by = NULL, by_col = NULL, cols = NULL)

Call structure

create_deleted_data() relies on the same four helpers as create_new_data(): anti_join_base(), select_cols(), rename_join_col() (which renames the join column), and create_new_column() (which builds the join column from the by columns, as shown in the create-new-data vignette). The call tree below was generated from the package source with stackcallr (pak::pak("mjfrigaard/stackcallr")). Only functions defined in dfdiffs are shown.

stackcallr::call_tree_dir("R", root = "create_deleted_data")
█─create_deleted_data
├─anti_join_base
├─select_cols
├─rename_join_col
└─create_new_column

Worked examples

No by column: matching whole rows

When we supply only the two datasets, create_deleted_data() treats a row in base as deleted if no row in compare has identical values across every shared column. The result below matches DeletedData:

create_deleted_data(
  compare = IncompleteData,
  base = CompleteData)

A single by column

First, we’ll use create_new_column() to build a join_var column from subject and record in both datasets:

CompleteDataJoin <- create_new_column(data = CompleteData,
  cols = c("subject", "record"),
  new_name = "join_var")
IncompleteDataJoin <- create_new_column(data = IncompleteData,
  cols = c("subject", "record"),
  new_name = "join_var")

Passing join_var as the by column matches rows on that key instead of on row position:

create_deleted_data(
  compare = IncompleteDataJoin,
  base = CompleteDataJoin,
  by = "join_var")

Multiple by columns, a new by_col, and cols

This is the most complete case. The by columns are combined into a single key named with by_col, and only the columns in cols are compared:

create_deleted_data(
  compare = IncompleteData,
  base = CompleteData,
  by = c('subject', 'record'),
  by_col = "new_join_col",
  cols = c("subject", "record", "text_var", "factor_var"))
